title: Individual influences on behavior

A) HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY

  • Biological bases: neurotransmitters (dopamine: reward, movement; serotonin: mood; GABA: inhibition; glutamate: excitation; acetylcholine: memory, muscle). Brain regions: frontal (executive), parietal (somatosensory, spatial), temporal (auditory, language comprehension), occipital (vision); limbic system (emotion, memory). Split-brain: left hemisphere usually controls speech, so an image shown to the left visual field (right hemisphere) cannot be named but can be selected by the left hand.
  • Genes and behavior: twin and adoption studies; heritability is population-level. Gene–environment interaction (epigenetics, diathesis–stress).
  • Personality theories:
  • Psychoanalytic (Freud: id, ego, superego; defense mechanisms). Neo-Freudians: Adler, Jung, Horney.
  • Humanistic (Rogers: unconditional positive regard, congruence; Maslow).
  • Trait (Big Five "OCEAN": openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism; Eysenck). Mischel's person–situation critique.
  • Social cognitive (Bandura: reciprocal determinism, self-efficacy; Rotter: locus of control).
  • Biological (temperament, Eysenck's arousal theory of extraversion).
  • Psychological disorders (DSM-5): depressive disorders (MDD: ≥ 2 weeks), bipolar (mania; lithium as mood stabilizer), anxiety disorders, OCD and related (body dysmorphic disorder), trauma-related (PTSD), schizophrenia (positive and negative symptoms; enlarged ventricles; dopamine hypothesis), dissociative, somatic, personality disorders (clusters A odd, B dramatic, C anxious), neurocognitive (delirium: acute, fluctuating attention; dementia: gradual). Biopsychosocial model.
  • Motivation: instinct, drive-reduction (homeostasis), arousal (optimal level), incentive theories; Maslow's hierarchy; self-determination theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness); intrinsic vs. extrinsic (overjustification effect). Hunger: lateral hypothalamus (start), ventromedial (stop); leptin and ghrelin.
  • Attitudes and behavior: ABC model (affective, behavioral, cognitive). Cognitive dissonance: behavior can change attitudes. Attitudes predict behavior best when strong, specific and accessible.

C) COMMON TRAPS + 3 MCAT-STYLE Qs

Trap 1: Heritability applies to individuals. A heritability of 0.6 does not mean 60% of any one person's trait comes from genes. It describes how much of the variation in a population tracks genetic variation, in that environment.

Trap 2: Delirium vs. dementia. Delirium is acute and fluctuating, with impaired attention, often from medication or infection, and is often reversible. Dementia is gradual and progressive.

Q1. A researcher pays children to draw with markers, an activity they already enjoyed. When payment stops, they draw less than before. Which concept explains this?

  • A) Drive-reduction theory
  • B) Overjustification effect
  • C) Cognitive dissonance
  • D) Learned helplessness

Answer: B. An external reward undermined intrinsic motivation.

  • A is wrong: drawing does not reduce a biological drive.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: dissonance would increase liking for a behavior done with insufficient reward.
  • D is wrong: learned helplessness follows uncontrollable negative events.

Q2. A patient hears voices commenting on her actions and believes neighbors are broadcasting her thoughts. She also has flat affect and little speech. Which symptom list is correct?

  • A) Positive: flat affect; negative: hallucinations
  • B) Positive: hallucinations and delusions; negative: flat affect and alogia
  • C) All four are negative symptoms
  • D) All four are positive symptoms

Answer: B. Positive symptoms add experiences (hallucinations, delusions); negative symptoms are deficits (flat affect, alogia, avolition).

  • A is wrong: it swaps the categories.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: hallucinations and delusions are positive.
  • D is wrong: flat affect and alogia are negative.

Q3. A student believes her exam grade depends mostly on luck and on the teacher's mood. Which concept describes this belief, and in which theory is it rooted?

  • A) External locus of control; Rotter's social learning theory
  • B) Low self-esteem; humanistic theory
  • C) Neuroticism; trait theory
  • D) Reaction formation; psychoanalytic theory

Answer: A. Attributing outcomes to outside forces is an external locus of control (Rotter).

  • A is correct.
  • B is wrong: self-esteem is self-evaluation, not beliefs about causes of outcomes.
  • C is wrong: neuroticism is emotional instability, a trait, not a causal belief.
  • D is wrong: reaction formation is acting opposite to an unacceptable impulse.
